world-92720765a4.headline: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
world-92720765a4.fulltext:
Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
- Published
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.
The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.
It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Russia has confirmed the meeting. China has yet to react.
No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.
Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.
"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.
She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".
A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation that helped resolve the Cold War.
The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement that included China, which has been building up its arsenal.
Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could create major hurdles and take years.
Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September.
Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.
But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.
Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan.
The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its largest trade partner.
Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.
Earlier this month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media that there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.

ai-703d5a8bd2.headline: OpenAI reassigns robotics researchers to other teams as general-purpose models might make specialized robotics AI unnecessary
ai-703d5a8bd2.fulltext:
OpenAI reassigns robotics researchers to other teams as general-purpose models might make specialized robotics AI unnecessary
Update –
The opening sentence of this article originally stated that OpenAI was "apparently disbanding its robotics team again." OpenAI has since clarified that it reorganized the team to work more closely with research and product and that robotics work continues. The opening sentence has been updated to reflect this.
OpenAI has reorganized its robotics team, though for different reasons than when it first disbanded the unit in 2020.
Rather than abandoning robotics, the company wants to accelerate it by folding researchers into other teams. Robotics researchers are moving to the main research team under Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams join Greg Brockman's Applied organization.
OpenAI made the decision on such short notice that it had already booked a booth at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin, which then sat empty, Fortune reports. OpenAI apparently believes that general-purpose models like GPT-6 Astra can control robots directly, reducing the need for specialized robotics models.
In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8 percent success rate on simulated robotics tasks, compared to 51 percent for the best specialized models. The tests used a simulated DROID robot, not a physical one.
A new robotics benchmark called StationeryBench compared GPT-6 Astra with Ai2's MolmoAct2 on five tasks involving desk objects on dual-arm YAM robotic arms. Across 200 trials, Astra fully completed 7 out of 100 tasks, while MolmoAct2 didn't complete a single one. Astra's average progress score was 46, compared to 12 for MolmoAct2. In another test, Astra running on a humanoid robot navigated and cleaned up a kitchen.
It remains unclear how much robotics data OpenAI and others incorporated during training. Other large general-purpose models from Anthropic and Google have also made recent progress on robotics tasks. Specialized robotics models may still have advantages in cost and reliability as well as speed and energy consumption, even if they don't generalize as well.
Yoav Artzi, an AI researcher at Cornell University and Google DeepMind, also sees Astra as a major leap in spatial understanding. On the still-unpublished REMAP benchmark, GPT-6 Astra reaches near-human accuracy, according to Artzi. He suspects that OpenAI may have trained the model on large amounts of 3D training data such as Blender scenes.
OpenAI and robots, it's complicated
OpenAI shut down its robotics division in 2020 because, according to co-founder Wojciech Zaremba, the company lacked the training data it needed and large language models were a faster path to AGI. The company rebuilt the team in 2024. CEO Sam Altman is reportedly targeting a first public robot demo for 2027, and OpenAI wants to build its own everyday robots in the long term. But the company also faces heavy financial pressure to focus on its core AI business, where it has lost significant ground to Anthropic.

india-4e561f7891.headline: Bulk of issues resolved, India-US trade pact approaching 'finishing line': Jaishankar
india-4e561f7891.fulltext:
India
Bulk of issues resolved, India-US trade pact approaching 'finishing line': Jaishankar
His remarks come ahead of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's likely visit to the US next month for the G20 Summit in Miami on December 14 and 15. 
NEW DELHI: India and the US have resolved most issues concerning their proposed trade agreement, including tariff lines, and the pact could be finalised soon, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said on Saturday, indicating that negotiations had reached their final stage.
Speaking at an interactive session at the HT Leadership Summit, Jaishankar said the remaining concerns were largely on the American side and expressed hope that both countries would conclude the negotiations shortly.
"It's certainly our hope, and in many ways anticipation, that we are at the last stretch. That's not a secret," he said, responding to a question on the progress of the trade talks.
"The hope is that we should close it out soon. It's always the case that in that last period, everybody's impatient," he added.
His remarks come ahead of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's likely visit to the US next month for the G20 Summit in Miami on December 14 and 15. Modi and US President Donald Trump are expected to discuss bilateral relations and the progress of the proposed trade pact on the sidelines of the summit.
Jaishankar said the bulk of the issues had been resolved, including tariff-related matters, after detailed negotiations between the two sides.
"If you are serious, you go tariff line by tariff line. That takes time. Now we've done it the painstaking way," he said, adding that the negotiations had reached "almost the finishing line".
The minister said India was seeking a trade agreement that was balanced, mutually beneficial and provided its goods with a comparative advantage over those from comparable economies.
"For us, the key is that we want a trade deal which is beneficial, it is balanced and which would give us a comparative advantage over groups of comparable economies," he said.
Describing the US as India's biggest market and the world's largest economy, Jaishankar said a trade agreement with Washington would benefit India. He added that the challenge was to find a mutually acceptable arrangement, given the US administration's efforts to secure bilateral trade deals.
The two countries have been negotiating the proposed agreement since early 2025 to address tariff-related differences, remove non-tariff barriers and improve market access.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had also said last month in Mumbai that both sides were close to finalising the agreement.
Jaishankar said trade negotiations involved serious economic considerations, including their implications for jobs and livelihoods, and could not be concluded through hurried decisions.
He also said India's recent free trade agreements had been more carefully assessed, both strategically and economically, compared with some of its earlier agreements with Asian economies.
The proposed trade deal assumes significance amid a downturn in India-US relations following Washington's imposition of punitive tariffs on Indian goods last year, Trump's claims about his role in de-escalating the India-Pakistan military conflict in May 2025, and differences over immigration policies and H-1B visa fees.
Tensions have also emerged over Washington's decision to restrict a green-card processing programme affecting major Indian IT companies, including Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro.

india-e23e1e824d.headline: India’s economy shows strength even as household inflation crosses 6 percent
india-e23e1e824d.fulltext:
India’s household inflation has moved above 6 percent for the first time in nearly two years, making everyday spending more difficult for families across the country. In October, the Consumer Price Index-based inflation rate rose to 6.09 percent, up from 5.54 percent in September. This was the twelfth consecutive month in which inflation increased, and it crossed the upper limit of the Reserve Bank of India’s inflation target.
The rise has been driven largely by higher food prices and an unfavourable base effect. A base effect simply means that prices are being compared with a relatively low level from the same month last year, which can make the current inflation number appear higher. However, the main concern is not only the statistical effect; food prices have been rising in a way that directly affects household budgets, especially for essentials such as vegetables, pulses, edible oils and other daily-use items.
The Reserve Bank of India is legally required to keep inflation around 4 percent, with a flexible range of 2 to 6 percent. Inflation has remained above 4 percent for five months in a row. The latest reading of 6.09 percent has now crossed the 6 percent upper boundary for the first time since October 2024. This makes price control a major priority for the central bank, because persistent inflation reduces the purchasing power of money and makes it harder for ordinary families to manage monthly expenses.
For households, the impact is very practical. When inflation rises, the same amount of money buys fewer goods and services than before. A family that spends a fixed amount on groceries, transport, school-related costs and household needs may find that its monthly budget no longer covers the same basket of items. Food inflation is especially important because food takes a large share of spending for many Indian households. Even a small increase in the price of essential food items can quickly change the overall household budget.
The pressure is now clearly on the RBI to act further. Last month, the central bank’s Monetary Policy Committee increased the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5 percent. Economists widely expect another rate hike at the committee’s next meeting, scheduled for December 2 to 4. A higher repo rate generally makes borrowing more expensive for banks, which can then pass on higher interest costs to borrowers.
This has a direct connection with common financial decisions. Home loan EMIs, vehicle loans, personal loans and credit-card interest can become costlier when lending rates rise. At the same time, higher interest rates may offer better returns on fixed deposits and savings instruments. However, for families already dealing with higher daily expenses, the benefit from higher deposit rates may not immediately offset the pressure created by costlier loans and rising prices.
The RBI’s latest forecast suggests that the inflation challenge may continue for some time. It expects CPI inflation to average 6 percent during October to December, 5.7 percent during January to March 2027, and 5.6 percent during April to June 2027. These projections indicate that inflation is likely to remain above the RBI’s 4 percent target in the coming quarters, even if it may ease gradually from the current high level.
What makes the situation more complicated is that the Indian economy continues to grow strongly. GDP growth in April to June was unexpectedly high at 7.8 percent, and economists expect a similar pace in July to September.
BofA Securities economists Rahul Bajoria and Smriti Mehra have projected 7.7 percent growth for the second quarter of 2026-27, higher than the RBI’s forecast of 7.2 percent and the Finance Ministry’s estimate of 7.35 percent. Strong growth usually supports jobs and incomes, but it can also keep demand high, which may make it harder to bring inflation down quickly.
There are also external risks. Global geopolitics can affect crude oil prices, and changes in oil prices often influence transport costs, production costs and ultimately consumer prices in India.
Weather-related risks, including the possible impact of El Nino, can also affect agricultural output and food supply. Since food inflation is a major driver of the current rise, any disruption in crop production, supply chains or rainfall patterns could keep prices elevated.
Economists at BofA Securities expect the RBI to increase interest rates by another 75 basis points over the next six to nine months. They believe this tightening cycle could raise credit costs and soften consumer demand at the margin.
In simple terms, costlier loans may reduce some spending on big-ticket purchases, while higher interest rates can help cool demand and control inflation. But this policy trade-off is delicate because excessive tightening could also slow economic growth.
The bigger message is that inflation is no longer only a number discussed by economists and policymakers. It is now visible in kitchen budgets, fuel expenses, loan repayments and monthly household planning.
With inflation above the RBI’s upper tolerance limit and food prices under pressure, the coming months will be important for both consumers and policymakers. The RBI faces the challenge of controlling prices without weakening the strong growth momentum in the economy.

ai-075bbfb634.headline: Asian governments react to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit
ai-075bbfb634.fulltext:
Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations.
On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed.
Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry.
China
China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday, a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang.
Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain.
Singapore
In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs.
The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration.
In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case.
South Korea
South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report.
Taiwan
Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media. Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project.
Japan
In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors.

india-deep-tech-b3b1310418.headline: Ukrainian defense tech startup hits $6 billion valuation as investors bet on battle-tested drones
india-deep-tech-b3b1310418.fulltext:
Ukrainian defense technology company UFORCE has raised $700 million in a funding round valuing it at $6 billion, as investor interest grows in autonomous weapons systems tested on the battlefield in Ukraine.
UFORCE, which develops unmanned aerial, maritime, and land systems as well as AI software used to coordinate them, raised $50 million at a valuation of around $1 billion in March.
The Series A round was co-led by Valor Equity Partners and the U.K.'s National Wealth Fund, with participation from investors across Silicon Valley, Europe and Asia, the company announced Thursday.
UFORCE CEO Oleg Rogynskyy told CNBC that the company's bookings have more than doubled over the past year, from a base of several hundred million dollars, but declined to disclose more exact figures.
He said the company's financial performance justified its latest valuation, adding that UFORCE had received offers from investors at even higher valuations.
"We were getting offers with much higher valuation, but we chose this one because of Valor and the rest of the investors," Rogynskyy said. “In terms of valuation to bookings, valuation to revenue, this is actually not an aggressive valuation.”
The company plans to use the new funding to scale manufacturing in Ukraine and in allied countries, including the U.S., Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East.
Startups across NATO and allied countries raised $27.1 billion through September, nearly double the total for all of 2025, according to an October report from Dealroom and Resilience Media.
Rogynskyy said UFORCE had already manufactured ten times as many unmanned surface vessels as the competitors it typically measures itself against, and was looking to increase manufacturing capacity substantially. CNBC could not independently verify the comparison.
The expansion comes as militaries around the world look to learn from the war in Ukraine, where relatively inexpensive drones are challenging the role of traditional military equipment like crewed tanks or fighter jets.
UFORCE says its NEMESIS drones have completed more than 300,000 combat flights, while its MAGURA naval vessels have contributed to the destruction of more than a dozen Russian warships in the Black Sea.
Rogynskyy said the company was already working with several NATO countries, but declined to identify its customers or disclose how much of its production was being supplied to Ukraine versus overseas markets.
Asked whether growing international demand could divert supplies away from Ukraine, he said the company was committed to meeting Ukrainian military requirements first.
"We are very careful about that, and we make sure that we deliver on all Ukrainian needs first and foremost," he said.
Modern warfare
Like many of its peers, UFORCE is seeking to challenge the economics of conventional warfare, arguing that large numbers of inexpensive autonomous systems can provide a significantly cheaper way of defense than more traditional weapons.
Rogynskyy said Ukrainian defense tech companies have an advantage over established Western manufacturers because their engineers receive continuous feedback from military personnel using their equipment on the battlefield.
"Speed of innovation, of course, is much faster with Ukrainian defense technology companies as compared to primes and Western defense techs," he said.
Looking further ahead, Rogynskyy predicted that autonomous systems would gradually replace much of the military equipment currently operated by humans, including aircraft and naval vessels.
He said he could not envision militaries continuing to purchase new crewed aircraft or frigates 10 years from now, although he acknowledged that conventional equipment such as F-35 fighter jets would remain important in the near term.

ai-2965a827d1.headline: Jensen Huang’s Exit: How Deep Does NVIDIA’s AI Ecosystem Run In India?
ai-2965a827d1.fulltext: Jensen Huang’s exit from NVIDIA has put the spotlight on the company’s leadership and succession plans. But for India, the more consequential question is what happens to an ecosystem that has increasingly come to depend on the American chipmaker for its AI ambitions. From data centre operators ordering thousands of GPUs to startups building on its software stack, NVIDIA has established relationships across almost every layer of India's AI industry. Its influence extends beyond hardware procurement to cloud infrastructure, developer tools, technical partnerships, startup incubation and even equity investments. It is also helping Indian companies access global investors and customers. The scale of this presence is visible in the country's expanding AI infrastructure ambitions. Some of the key partnerships include Yotta Data Services committing to deploying more than 20,000 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs, while Greenko promoters-backed AM Intelligence (AMI) has announced orders for 29,000 next-generation Rubin GPUs. L&T's Vyoma, meanwhile, is developing a 10,000-GPU AI Factory using NVIDIA's B300 architecture. But these relationships are not identical. Some companies procure hardware, others access NVIDIA's technology through OEMs and systems integrators, while several startups rely primarily on its software and developer ecosystem. India's dependence on NVIDIA runs across three layers: hardware, software and commercial relationships. Competing with NVIDIA and providing alternatives to its Indian partners, therefore, requires more than matching its hardware. Rivals must also replicate its software ecosystem and industry relationships, Sanchit Vir Gogoi, analyst and founder of Greyhound Research, told Inc42. The question is whether Huang's departure changes any of these relationships, and how exposed Indian companies are to a change in NVIDIA's priorities. NVIDIA's Grip On AI Compute India's AI infrastructure buildout is increasingly being shaped around NVIDIA's GPUs. Yotta, Neysa, ESDS, AMI, E2E Networks and L&T Vyoma are among the companies making large commitments to the chipmaker's hardware, although the procurement arrangements and partnerships differ. According to Counterpoint Research, quoted by Moneycontrol, there have been commitments of over $4–5 Bn toward Nvidia's GPU-powered AI data centres. This included both AI stack and infrastructure partnerships. That dependence also has a policy dimension. The IndiaAI Mission's common compute programme relies on a network of empanelled cloud and infrastructure providers. IndiaAI Mission, which had onboarded over 45,000 GPUs by June 2026. By August, it had approved 237 projects for subsidised compute, with 93.18 Lakh GPU hours sanctioned. Any disruption in access to advanced GPUs could therefore affect not just private data centre operators but also the availability and pricing of compute for startups, researchers and government-backed AI projects. The Geopolitical GPU Game Huang's exit has exposed a geopolitical vulnerability in India's AI infrastructure ambitions: its dependence on a company whose access to global markets, political influence and supply chains is now under greater scrutiny. The concern is particularly relevant amid renewed US scrutiny of advanced chip exports. The Biden administration's 2025 AI Diffusion Rule, which had placed India in a middle tier with import caps, was subsequently suspended from enforcement by the Trump administration. However, the formal rescission process remains incomplete, according to a May 2026 Government Accountability Office assessment, as noted by Vipul Agrawal, partner at law firm Clavius Legal. More recently, reports have suggested that the US Commerce Department is considering tighter licensing requirements for advanced chip shipments to seven countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand. India has not been named in the proposed framework so far. Agrawal says India's current position is comparatively favourable, but that does not guarantee uninterrupted access. "On the US Government's published position, India currently enjoys comparatively favourable treatment for buying advanced AI chips, but that is not a guarantee of supply. Suppliers may ask more about where chips are deployed, who the customers are and where the chips may go next, which could slow procurement." He adds that Indian operators must also account for restrictions governing the subsequent transfer or export of controlled hardware. Exports of certain high-performance chips and computers containing these chipsets are only allowed on government authorisation. For Indian neoclouds and data centre operators, the challenge is therefore not limited to securing an initial GPU shipment. They must also understand the ownership structure of their customers, intended use and potential restrictions on overseas customers accessing their infrastructure. “Indian neoclouds and data centre operators must assess their obligations under the US Export Administration Regulations (EAR). This includes verifying the export classification of the GPUs, applicable licensing requirements, and the identity of the supplier, consignee, and end-user,” said Shashi Mathews, partner At CMS INDUSLAW. Indian providers must bear in mind that providing foreign nationals or restricted entities with access to controlled technology or computing power can legally function similarly to exporting the physical item, he added. Who Can Compete With NVIDIA? Meanwhile, alternatives are beginning to emerge. AMD's Instinct accelerators and Google's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) offer competing architectures. The IndiaAI Compute Portal's empanelment table lists 44,077 compute units from 14 bidders: 35,985 NVIDIA units, 5,548 Google Trillium TPUs, 1,096 AMD MI300X and MI325X units, 1,200 AWS Trainium and Inferentia units, and 248 Intel Gaudi units. So does India need to diversify? “Yes, by workload, and with evidence,” said Greyhound Research’s Gogoi. “Inference is where portability is closest to ready, because serving software increasingly hides the accelerator from the application.” Indian startups are also exploring different approaches. Bengaluru-based Turiyam is developing a full-stack compute platform built around inference workloads, CUDA-free middleware and RISC-V hardware. Ziroh Labs, meanwhile, is positioning its Kompact AI runtime as a CPU-first alternative, claiming NVIDIA A100-class inference performance on Intel Xeon processors. These companies are not yet substitutes for NVIDIA's large-scale GPU ecosystem. But they reflect an emerging effort to reduce dependence on a single hardware architecture. The NVIDIA Ecosystem Lock-In Hardware is only one part of NVIDIA's influence. Its software, particularly CUDA, is arguably an even more significant source of competitive advantage. CUDA, NVIDIA's parallel computing platform, allows developers to build applications that run on its GPUs. Over the years, the company has built an extensive ecosystem of libraries, development tools and frameworks around it, including cuDNN, TensorRT and its broader AI Enterprise platform. For companies developing and deploying AI models, this ecosystem reduces the time and effort required to build applications on NVIDIA hardware. Developers can use established frameworks and libraries rather than building infrastructure from scratch. This creates a significant switching cost. A company that has invested years in building its AI applications around CUDA cannot necessarily move to AMD or another accelerator simply by replacing its GPUs. It may have to rewrite parts of its software, optimise workloads and retrain engineering teams. NVIDIA has also expanded its software offerings beyond the underlying computing platform. Its NeMo framework supports the development and customisation of generative AI models, while NIM provides microservices for deploying AI models in production. The company has also developed Nemotron, a family of open models, and tools for data curation and model optimisation. And Indian companies are already using these offerings. NVIDIA has Sarvam AI, Gnani.ai, Chariot, CoRover.ai, and Tech Mahindra among adopters of its NeMo and Nemotron ecosystem. TCS, Infosys and Wipro have also been building enterprise AI solutions using NVIDIA's software stack. This software presence is significant because it creates relationships even with companies that do not directly own or operate large GPU clusters. Will Open Source Survive? Jensen Huang has also championed open source AI models and development tools, an approach that has helped NVIDIA strengthen its position among developers. Notably, NVIDIA announced that it will acquire Huggingface, one of the world’s largest repositories of open source models, for approximately $13 Bn. However, its support for open source is also commercially driven. Open models can be adapted and optimised to run on the hardware most widely available to developers. Given NVIDIA's current market position, this often means its own GPUs and CUDA cores. Rahul Sai Poruri, CEO of FOSS United Foundation, which supports and promotes open source ecosystem in India, believes NVIDIA's strategy to drive open source is unlikely to change dramatically after Huang's departure. "NVIDIA definitely benefits significantly from the existence of open models. If we have more and more closed models, such as Google's Gemini, these models could be optimised specifically for Google's hardware, including its TPUs. Open models, on the other hand, are likely to be optimised for whatever GPU is most widely available to developers. Currently, that is NVIDIA." He added that it could take several years, potentially half a decade or more, for the broader ecosystem to meaningfully reduce its dependence on NVIDIA. Huang's exit may change the company's public positioning or priorities over time. However, its software business, developer relationships and established integrations are institutional assets that are unlikely to disappear with a leadership transition. From Inception To Startup Investments NVIDIA's relationship with India extends beyond selling hardware and software; the company has also been building a pipeline of startups, investors and technology partners that can expand the adoption of its computing platforms. A key part of this strategy is NVIDIA Inception, its global startup programme. The initiative provides early-stage companies with access to technical training, developer tools, preferred pricing on select hardware and software, cloud credits and introductions to potential investors and business partners. The programme is free and does not require startups to give up equity. NVIDIA says it supports more than 4,000 Indian AI startups, making it an important channel for bringing new developers and companies into its ecosystem. More recently, NVIDIA has started making direct equity investments in Indian startups. In August 2026, it participated in a $74 Mn funding tranche for Sarvam AI, becoming the startup's first strategic investor from the global chip industry. The investment came as Sarvam expanded its efforts to build sovereign AI models and applications for Indian languages. NVIDIA also participated in Simplismart's $14 Mn Series B round in October 2026. The startup builds software to help enterprises deploy and optimise AI models and has worked with NVIDIA on technical integrations involving its Dynamo inference software. These investments are important because they go beyond the traditional customer-vendor relationship. NVIDIA is now backing companies that could become significant consumers of its hardware and software, while also helping them develop products and reach customers. Anthropic CEO Amodei admits "there's a huge uncertainty in what's going to happen next year" days before a record IPO
Key Points
- Ahead of Anthropic's planned IPO, CEO Dario Amodei called buying compute "the deepest business dilemma" his company faces, noting that capacity has to be purchased one to two years before anyone knows whether revenue will justify the cost.
- Anthropic's commitments have reached nearly $901 billion, according to Bloomberg, most of it tied to compute and chips, with roughly $71 billion coming due by September 2027 alone.
- The IPO is designed to build a cash buffer large enough to carry the company through a potential mismatch between spending and revenue.
Days before what could be the largest IPO in history, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei names the central weakness of his business model. Nobody knows how the company's compute investments will pay off, he says. It isn't the first time he's sounded this warning.
"There's a huge uncertainty in what's going to happen next year." Speaking at a JPMorgan Chase investor event in New York on Friday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei used that line to sum up the problem facing his company.
The admission came, of all times, in the last days before the company's planned Nov. 19 IPO, and compute was one of several topics in the conversation. Speaking with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon, he said, "Compute is the deepest business dilemma that the company faces."
AI technology is advancing so fast that, Amodei said, no one yet knows how that progress will translate into economic value. But compute has to be bought one to two years ahead, before anyone knows whether revenue will justify the cost.
If Anthropic buys too little, he said, it won't have the resources for customers and new technologies, and revenue takes a hit. Buying too much carries the opposite risk. "You can financially overextend yourself," Amodei said.
$901 billion bet on an uncertain future
Anthropic has already committed nearly $901 billion, most of it to compute and chips, according to Bloomberg. Roughly $71 billion of that comes due by September 2027. Bloomberg notes that figure exceeds the market cap of about two-thirds of S&P 500 companies.
Back in February 2026, Amodei warned in much sharper terms that he could buy $1 trillion of compute starting at the end of 2027 and go bankrupt if revenue fell short. Being off by just one year could mean bankruptcy. He is not sure some competitors have done the math, and he said they don't really understand the risks they're taking. The stakes have kept rising since then.
Anthropic wants the IPO to cushion against the unknown
Amodei described two ways Anthropic softens the compute dilemma: gross margins and cash on the balance sheet. He said the company’s gross margins are "quite good," especially compared with other players, and that Anthropic has a large cash balance and is seeking to raise more.
The company also buys relatively little compute upfront, then can turn to the spot market for additional capacity if business goes better than expected. Amodei compared that approach to buying insurance, saying it leaves Anthropic covered if results fall short while allowing it to invest more when things go well.
The compute bets were the biggest reason to go public: the more cash Anthropic holds, he said, the wider its margin for error between a world with too little compute and one with too much.
Anthropic plans to raise up to $64.4 billion through the IPO and another $26 billion through a private placement, Bloomberg reports. Combined, that would make it the largest IPO ever. The offering is reportedly already about six times oversubscribed.
Anthropic's annualized revenue run rate hit $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from late September, according to company filings. Bloomberg says the rising popularity of AI products, including its coding models, has helped fuel revenue growth.
Amodei struck a relaxed tone about the IPO's timing, saying he wasn't fixated on a specific month or particular market conditions. Anthropic, he noted, grew from nothing to its current size in just six years. The most common advice he got before the IPO, or the advice that resonated most, he said, was something like "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's really worth." That, he said, is very similar to a model Anthropic uses internally: "under-promise and over-deliver."
In the same conversation, though, Amodei said he hopes AI will cure cancer and Alzheimer's within five to 15 years, adding that he doesn't know exactly. In Silicon Valley, that may already count as under-promising.

ai-1c4e572d1e.headline: Runway's open-source Praxis-1 turns video AI into a robot controller
ai-1c4e572d1e.fulltext:
Runway's open-source Praxis-1 turns video AI into a robot controller
Key Points
- Runway has released its robot model Praxis-1 with open weights and source code under the Apache 2.0 license.
- Trained on videos and robot data, the model processes camera images, text instructions, and position data to calculate matching robot movements.
- Praxis-1 can be adapted to new robot systems through additional training, according to Runway. The model does occasionally confuse similar-looking objects, though, and it can't yet reliably plan complex action sequences on its own.
AI company Runway has released its robot model Praxis-1 with open weights and source code. The model uses what it learned from video to control robots and shows promising results in the company's own tests.
Runway has released Praxis-1, its AI model for controlling robots. The company first introduced Praxis-1 in late September but initially gave access only to select partners. Alongside the release, Runway published a detailed research report with new performance tests.
Runway's model weights and source code are available under the Apache 2.0 license, which allows commercial use.
Praxis-1 takes in camera images, text instructions, and information about a robot's position. From those inputs, it predicts how the environment will change and calculates the right robot movements. As new camera frames come in, the model continuously adjusts its control.
Praxis-1 builds on video training to control robots
Praxis-1 builds on a video model that learned how objects move and interact from ordinary footage. Runway then fine-tuned it with videos of human actions and robot data. This approach could reduce the need for expensive robot-specific datasets, which have traditionally been collected just to train these kinds of systems.
Runway is best known for generative video models like Gen-4.5. With Praxis-1, the company is bringing its video research into robotics. Runway calls Praxis-1 a World Action Model that predicts how a scene will change and derives matching robot movements from those predictions. Since September, robotics companies Standard Bots, Noble Machines, and Ultra have been testing Praxis-1 on different systems, including a humanoid robot, an industrial robot arm, and a dual-arm warehouse robot.
Praxis-1 leads among World Action Models
Praxis-1 still needs some specialized robot data. To adapt it to a Franka robot arm, Runway used about 277 hours of recordings from the public DROID research dataset, according to its research report. Those recordings show robots grasping and moving objects, for example. For a dual-arm robot, the company used between 1,400 and 2,600 hours of training material. Runway had already used DROID data and data from other robot systems during earlier training stages. Whether the approach actually needs less robot data overall than comparable models without general video pretraining is still an open question.
On Nvidia's RoboLab-120 leaderboard, Praxis-1 scores a 46.2 percent success rate. The benchmark tests how reliably robot models can sort, grasp, or stack objects across 120 tasks in simulation. FLUX 3 Action, also built as a World Action Model, scores 42.9 percent under the same test conditions. That puts Praxis-1 at the top of the World Action Model category. In the overall leaderboard, it ranks fifth behind two AI agents and two robot models with different architectures. Runway ran all the tests itself, and the results haven't been independently verified yet.
After fine-tuning on DROID data, Runway tested the model on a real Franka robot arm. Both models had to complete the same ten tasks, like placing a banana on a plate or closing a drawer. With ten attempts per task, Praxis-1 succeeded 88 times, while FLUX 3 Action managed 80.
Runway also tested how well Praxis-1 transfers to a robot type it had never seen before, using data from a mobile robot platform with a gripper arm that Google had previously used to develop RT-1. Recordings from this robot weren't part of Praxis-1's earlier training. After fine-tuning on about 95 hours of robot data, the model hit an average success rate of 80 percent in simulated tests, according to Runway. The tests covered four types of tasks, including grabbing soda cans, opening and closing drawers, and placing an apple in a drawer. Google's original RT-1 model scored 52.4 percent on the same benchmark.
Praxis-1 still has clear limits
Developers can download Praxis-1 from Hugging Face after signing up and agreeing to the access terms. The code is on GitHub. According to Runway's announcement, pre-adapted versions for different robots are already available alongside the base model. The base model needs additional training before it can work with new robot systems.
The standard model version needs a GPU with 80 GB of memory. A compressed version should fit on an RTX 5090 with 32 GB of VRAM based on Runway's memory estimates, though the actual peak memory usage hasn't been measured yet according to the GitHub docs.
The model sometimes confuses similar-looking objects and struggles with vague instructions, according to Runway's research report. For longer tasks, individual steps need to be spelled out because Praxis-1 can't reliably plan complex action sequences on its own yet.
Runway sees Praxis-1 primarily as a system for fast execution of robot movements. In the future, it could work alongside general-purpose AI models that break complex tasks down into individual steps.

ai-acaf00569e.headline: Where was Nvidia’s security team?
ai-acaf00569e.fulltext:
Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees.
At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago.
Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew.
Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions.
Not all of those relationships are the business of the security team. Relationships with subordinates typically fall to HR, legal, and the board. But an affair with an executive at a company under federal investigation is a different animal. (Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.) Security specialists say affairs can create vulnerabilities that foreign intelligence services look to exploit.
Catching that kind of exposure isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals.
Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week. (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct. The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him, and Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security.
Even if it had reached Nvidia’s security team, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, said a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said.
Many companies also define security very narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill, Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.”
Still, some of it is beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone.
What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.”
The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks.
Technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades said, pointing to IMSI catchers are one example. These devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more.
Eftimiades says no one knows yet if these were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But either way, what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, should become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed.
In the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.”

Search the way you think. Try our AI-powered search to find news faster.
Before Xi and Trump’s Apec meeting, what’s on hold – and what’s on the table?
China could retaliate with tighter rare earth export controls if Washington further restricts chip sales in the wake of the Nvidia saga, Chinese analysts say, though they expect broader US-China trade talks to remain on track ahead of a planned meeting between the two countries’ leaders next week.
Following Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia on Thursday amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs, attention now turns to whether Washington will further tighten semiconductor export controls on China.
US politicians seeking to exploit the Nvidia controversy during the trade talks to pressure Beijing would be “completely miscalculating”, according to Victor Gao, vice-president of the Beijing-based think tank Centre for China and Globalisation.
“What they may do is force China to tighten control of rare earths exports,” he said.
Huang admitted over the weekend to being unfaithful to his wife. The New York Times reported earlier that he had shared a close relationship with businesswoman Alice Huang, whom US officials suspect of being a Chinese operative. Beijing has repeatedly denied the spying allegations.
Alice Huang is a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which the US is investigating for allegedly playing a role in diverting advanced Nvidia artificial intelligence chips into China, where they are restricted for sale.
China used to be a key market for Nvidia, before an intensifying technology rivalry with Beijing led Washington to bar the company from selling its most advanced chips there in 2022.
Gao said the restrictions disrupted Nvidia’s long-standing business relationships in China, prompting Jensen Huang to repeatedly lobby the US government to restore chip sales to the country, where demand remained high.
Tighter restrictions could push China closer towards achieving semiconductor self-sufficiency over the next few years, before becoming a major chip exporter itself, Gao added.
Wang Yingliang, a Shanghai-based political economist and chief editor of economic analysis platform Sharp Voices, said that by making Jensen Huang’s personal affairs a security issue, the US had fresh justification for clamping down on its AI chip exports to China.
But Beijing could retaliate with sanctions on American companies, Wang said, or negotiate concessions on chip exports through broader trade discussions or cooperation on rare earths, drug trafficking and telecoms fraud.
“I do not believe that chips will have a significant impact on trade negotiations,” Wang said, adding that China’s substantial chip inventories and growing domestic technological capabilities could cushion the short-term impact of further restrictions.
China’s foreign ministry said on Friday that Beijing had consistently opposed the abuse of export controls, adding that further restrictions on Chinese access to American computing power would disrupt global supply chains.
“China and the United States should work together to implement the important consensus reached by their leaders and maintain the momentum of stable development in bilateral economic and trade relations,” spokeswoman Mao Ning said.
President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are expected to meet next week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen – their third meeting this year.
Ahead of the leaders’ meeting, another round of trade talks between the two sides is expected, where topics including reciprocal tariff cuts, agricultural purchases and rare earths are likely to be on the table.
Gao similarly downplayed the impact of the Nvidia case on US-China relations, noting that the two countries faced more pressing geopolitical issues.
“There are so many other things above Nvidia chips, above Jensen Huang, above Alice Huang, that China and the United States need to care about,” Gao said, adding that global conflicts and other issues were expected to be higher on the agenda in Shenzhen, especially with Trump and Xi also expected to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Xu Tianchen, an economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, however, argued that relations between China and the US could become more fragile, especially after the Republicans’ defeat in the recent US midterm elections.
“The ‘constructive strategic stability’ is essentially one between China and Trump, and Trump is now weakened,” said Xu, who was also of the view that Beijing was likely to further restrict exports of rare earths if the US imposed stricter chip controls.
The Nvidia issue has raised scrutiny from China hawks in Washington, with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick under fire over his oversight of chip sales to China.
Trump himself had largely remained supportive of Jensen Huang, having called him on Tuesday to urge him to fight for his job, The New York Times reported.
Wang said uncertainties remained over the US investigations into Alice Huang and potential opposition from Democrats in Congress. But barring any further escalation of national security concerns, he said he expected the Trump administration to continue adhering to its current chip export policy.
“Ultimately, whatever happens, it will depend on Trump’s own position,” Wang said.

New Delhi: The first Tejas Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Mark-1A (Mk1A) is likely to be handed over to the Indian Air Force (IAF) early in 2027, possibly as soon as January, a source in the know told ThePrint Thursday, on condition of anonymity.
State-run aerospace and defence company Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) missed the original February 2024 deadline to begin deliveries of the first tranche of 83 Mk1A jets, contracted for Rs 36,400 crore in February 2021. The slippage was attributed primarily to delays in the arrival of the F404-IN20 engines from American manufacturer GE Aerospace. The complex process of integrating weapons and systems has also affected the project. Deliveries of the first tranche were originally scheduled to be completed by February 2028.
In September 2025, HAL received a follow-on order for a second tranche of 97 Mk1A aircraft, worth over Rs 62,370 crore. Deliveries under this contract are expected to begin in financial year 2027-28 and conclude over six years.
By September this year, American engine maker GE Aerospace, headquartered in Evendale, Ohio, United States, had shipped a total of 14 F404-IN20 engines to HAL for the Tejas Mk1A fleet. They were supplied under a 2021 deal for 99 engines. The first engine arrived only in March 2025, although deliveries were originally slated to begin in 2023.
“Two requirements related to the Tejas Mk1A had been pending, including one or two functions or capabilities linked to the Israeli-origin radar. The software and integration issues are being fixed. Some concessions from the IAF may be involved. These will be addressed after the first one or two jets are handed over, informed by the IAF’s use of the jet,” said the source.
“The programme appears to be on the cusp of meeting certain major requirements,” the source said. “If everything goes to plan, the first one or two jets could be handed over in January itself, ahead of the Aero India 2027 aerospace and defence exhibition.”
Aero India, the country’s flagship biennial aerospace exhibition, is organised by the Ministry of Defence’s Department of Defence Production, and held at Air Force Station Yelahanka in Bengaluru. Its 16th edition will run from 8 to 12 February 2027.
The IAF has previously indicated that it is willing to relax some requirements temporarily to ease the Tejas Mk1A’s induction, provided they are met within a set time-frame. The remaining requirements are now close to being met, and their certification is not far off.
A company source declined to say when the first jets would be handed over to the IAF. The source did indicate, however, that the service and the defence public sector undertaking were working towards induction with strengthened coordination. “The IAF project management team, HAL and the certification agency are all involved in the process,” the company source added.
The development follows remarks by Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit, who took charge as the 29th Chief of the Air Staff at the end of October. The day after assuming office, he named the homegrown Tejas Mk1A and Mk2 fighters and the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), together with Indian-made sensors and weapons, as the IAF’s “highest priority”. “We will fight with Indian solutions,” Dixit said, adding that the force would field these systems in large enough numbers to sustain prolonged operations. Bringing the IAF’s combat strength back up towards its sanctioned level, he said, would be his “foremost task”.
HAL has to meet the Air Staff Qualitative Requirements (ASQRs) agreed for the Mk1A jets. ASQRs are specific, documented standards, qualifications and performance metrics that equipment must meet to fulfil operational requirements.
The Israeli ELTA EL/M-2052 active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar was originally meant to equip only a part of the 83 jets ordered in the first tranche, with the remainder to be fitted with the Defence Research and Development Organisation’s (DRDO) Uttam AESA radar. In 2025, however, HAL decided to fit all 83 jets in the first tranche with the EL/M-2052, owing to the time being taken to certify the Uttam.
The Mk1A is an improved variant of the indigenous Tejas Mk1, which is already operational with the IAF. A 4.5-generation fighter, it comes equipped with an AESA radar, the standard for modern fighter radars. Instead of a single antenna that has to be physically moved, an AESA radar uses hundreds of small transmitter-receiver modules whose beams are steered electronically. This lets it scan faster, track several targets at once, detect adversaries at longer ranges and resist jamming better.
The Mk1A also carries beyond-visual-range (BVR) missiles, which can strike enemy aircraft too far away for the pilot to see, so adversaries can be engaged from greater distances. Its electronic warfare suite protects it against adversary sensors and weapons. And because it can be refuelled in mid-air, the jet can reach more distant targets and patrol an area for longer before it has to return to base.
The Tejas Mk2, envisaged as an even more advanced variant that will be heavier and run on more powerful GE engines, is yet to fly in prototype form.
The AMCA, for its part, is India’s stealth combat aircraft in development. It is being pursued through an industry partnership model, and the process of picking the company or consortium that will help develop and build its prototypes is under way.
There are three contenders: the Tata Group, and two consortia, led by the Kalyani Group and Larsen & Toubro (L&T) respectively. Whichever of them wins, HAL’s monopoly on making combat aircraft will come to an end. Viewed this way, the AMCA programme is an effort to create a second combat aircraft production line in India, alongside HAL’s capacity.
The start of inductions of the Tejas Mk1A matters all the more because the IAF is at its lowest strength in 60 years, with 29 active fighter squadrons against the sanctioned 42.

indian-startups-66f1a4a70f.headline: Crunchbase Data: Nvidia’s Startup Funding Deals Hit A Record. What’s Next After Huang?
indian-startups-66f1a4a70f.fulltext:
Before it was thrust into crisis this week, Nvidia was steadily continuing its pace as one of the busiest startup investors around, including backing many of the biggest venture deals of 2026.
The chipmaker and its NVentures arm have participated in more than 120 startup funding deals so far this year, according to Crunchbase data, already topping last year’s record-setting pace and marking its most prolific year yet as a private-company investor.
With co-founder Jensen Huang’s sudden departure this week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs including with employees and a woman U.S. intelligence experts suspect of spying for China, we took a fresh look at where Nvidia and NVentures have been investing and what the future could hold.
A widening investment footprint
Nvidia is the most active corporate investor so far in 2026, an analysis of Crunchbase data shows. It and NVentures together are also among the top 20 most active investors in startups this year overall.
Nvidia’s startup investments this year total 121 and span AI model developers, data center operators, robotics startups and healthcare companies. That continues the broad approach we examined last year, when the company and its venture arm participated in 91 known startup financings, up from 54 the year prior.
The largest Nvidia-backed deals in 2026 include OpenAI’s Series G, which closed at $122 billion in March, and Anthropic’s $30 billion Series G in February. (Those figures represent the entire rounds, including other investors’ contributions, rather than Nvidia’s individual checks.)
The company also participated in a $3.9 billion September Series F for AI infrastructure provider Crusoe and a roughly $3.5 billion September Series D for model developer Mistral AI.
Of course, large as those deals are, Nvidia’s startup bets represent a small fraction of the company’s incredible market capitalization. Even as its share price tumbled this week with Huang’s departure and the surrounding news, Nvidia’s valuation remains close to $4 trillion.
Beyond the biggest AI labs
NVentures’ activity shows how far that investment footprint extends beyond the best-known model developers.
The venture arm’s larger bets this year include robot intelligence developer Skild AI’s $1.4 billion January Series C, and autonomous driving startup Waabi’s $750 million Series C in the same month. It also backed two rounds for Bedrock Robotics, which develops technology to automate construction equipment: a $270 million Series B in February and a $600 million Series C in October. Its healthcare investments included a $150 million April Series E for medical imaging AI company Aidoc.
As in years past, Nvidia and NVentures usually participate alongside other investors. The company or its venture arm are listed as lead or co-lead investors in about 1 in 5 of its deals this year, per Crunchbase data.
For startups, Nvidia’s value as an investor also extends beyond its deep pockets. NVentures describes its offering as access to technical teams, technology integrations and help reaching customers.
The question of what comes next
Nvidia’s new leadership could bring a different approach to risk. Before this week’s news, CFO and now interim CEO Collette Kress had pushed back on Huang’s increasingly large AI investments, Reuters reported this week, citing two people familiar with the matter.
Nvidia’s board has said it expects operations, customer commitments and its product roadmap to continue without interruption. That assurance leaves the pace of future investments an open question. With earnings scheduled for Nov. 17, founders and investors will be watching for signs of how much of Huang’s investment playbook continues under new leadership.

indian-startups-cbf22493d8.headline: AI could disrupt India's outsourcing model. It could also create millions of new exporters
indian-startups-cbf22493d8.fulltext:
AI could disrupt India's outsourcing model. It could also create millions of new exporters
AI is letting small Indian teams win global work that once needed a big company. As AI separates capability from headcount, it could shape India’s next export story.
I recently spoke to someone running a small creative agency from a Tier II Indian city, with most of his clients outside India. When AI came up, I expected him to talk about producing more content, faster. What he described was more interesting.
Rotoscoping, repetitive edits and parts of project management were now largely automated. His tiny team now takes on projects that once needed outside freelancers.
This is usually told as a productivity story. I think something more fundamental is happening: AI is changing how big a company must become before it can sell sophisticated services to the world.
For India, that is both an opportunity and an uncomfortable question.
The model that built India's services industry is changing
India’s services exports reached $421.3 billion in FY26, up from $387.5 billion a year earlier, with IT and business services the largest contributors. For three decades, the IT services industry ran on a simple equation: win more customers, hire more people.
AI challenges that. Coding, testing, research, documentation and customer support are the backbone of Indian outsourcing, and they are exactly where AI is improving fastest.
NASSCOM estimates that India’s tech industry earned $10-12 billion from AI services in FY26, while overall revenue grew 6.1% to $315 billion. Hiring continues, but total headcount rose just 2.3%. The link between revenue and people is loosening.
That threatens a model built on selling human capacity. Seen from a five-person company, the same shift looks very different.
AI reduces the minimum scale needed to compete
Small services firms have always faced a capacity problem: winning a large project meant building the organisation to deliver it. AI is beginning to separate capability from headcount.
I saw this first-hand when I spoke to the founder of a growth-marketing firm with 15 people and 22 AI agents, serving clients across more than seven countries. Its founder sorts every task into three buckets. Manual tasks, such as discovery calls, are deliberately kept away from AI. In AI-assisted tasks, AI does 85-95% of the work and a person checks the rest. Fully automated tasks, such as market research, run end to end and the only human step is sending the report to the client. About 40% of the firm’s budget goes to AI agents and software rather than headcount. The founder says it runs at 60-70% margins, against 20-25% for a typical agency.
Even discovery has changed. One UK client told the same growth-marketing founder that he found, evaluated and signed the firm within a single Perplexity chat.
We are beginning to see this from the payment layer
Building in cross-border payments, we see thousands of Indian businesses being paid from abroad, and what stands out is how small many of them are. Over the last 12 months, 347 solo professionals each collected more than $100,000 from overseas clients, and 117 teams of two to ten people each crossed $250,000.
The base is widening too. Exporters actively billing overseas customers each quarter grew roughly fivefold over seven quarters, from about 2,800 to 13,900. Some of that growth reflects more businesses coming onto our network, not just new exporters entering the market. But the median invoice stayed near $1,500 throughout, which suggests many more people are selling, rather than a few landing bigger deals. Eighty-two per cent of these exporters have ten or fewer people.
Exporters in AI, machine learning, data or automation grew about ninefold, and their median invoice is nearly double. They are roughly 2% of volume, so this is a direction, not yet a trend. One of them, a solo AI and machine-learning consultant, billed about $266,000 to US clients in 12 months from just four buyers. That is not typical, but a decade ago that work would have needed a firm.
Selling expertise, not capacity
If India’s response to AI is simply to perform the same outsourced work with fewer people and charge customers less, we may improve productivity without fundamentally improving our position in the global value chain.
The larger opportunity is to move from selling capacity to selling expertise and outcomes.
AI can analyse 500 customer conversations. It cannot independently decide which customer problem a business should build its future around. It can generate software. Someone still has to understand what should be built, how it fits into a customer’s organisation, and take responsibility when it doesn’t work.
The value increasingly lies in asking the right questions, applying domain knowledge, exercising judgement and owning the result.
This may actually make deep expertise more valuable, not less. Consider the Indian professional who has spent 15 years understanding insurance claims, semiconductor design, pharmaceutical regulation, supply chains or financial risk. That person can now combine their domain knowledge with tools that dramatically expand what one person can execute.
India has no shortage of such people. According to the Economic Survey 2024-25, the country accounts for 28% of the world’s STEM workforce and 23% of global software engineering talent. New kinds of work are already emerging. I find this example striking: a medical professional in Kochi spends her week marking organs and flagging anomalies in foetal ultrasound scans. She isn’t treating patients directly; she’s helping train AI systems being built for hospitals in the US.
A five-person global company cannot have a 50-person back office.
There is one problem.
India’s export framework was designed for firms with finance teams. Proof-of-export documentation, GST filings, foreign exchange conversion and bank reconciliation all assume someone in the back office is handling them.
A five-person firm billing clients in California and London, in multiple currencies, has no such person. Yet it may have hundreds of thousands of dollars moving across borders every year.
If AI shrinks the team needed to deliver the work, but the founder still loses hours each month to paperwork and compliance, the bottleneck has simply moved. Regulators, banks and the wider fintech ecosystem need to make cross-border compliance as lightweight as the businesses it now serves.
India’s next services giants may not look like giants
India’s first services-export era was built by assembling millions of skilled people into large organisations. That model isn’t disappearing. But the next phase may look much less concentrated: thousands, perhaps eventually many more, of specialist Indian businesses selling their expertise to the world.
The agency I spoke to is interesting not because AI helps it edit videos faster. It is interesting because a handful of people in an Indian city can now compete for work anywhere in the world.
Twenty-five years ago, India's services-export breakthrough was partly about proving that global work could be done from India.
The AI-era opportunity may be proving that you no longer need to build a large company to do a large amount of it.
Srivatsan Sridhar is Co-Founder and CEO of Skydo.

     India’s renewable energy sector attracted investments worth around $5.3 billion, or more than ₹50,000 crore, during the July-September 2026 period, aided by supportive policy pushes and deepening domestic markets.
The Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) said investments in India’s RE sector reached $5.28 billion (₹ 50,241 crore) in Q3 2026, up 21 per cent q-o-q from $4.35 billion ( ₹41,351 crore) in Q2 2026.
On an annual basis, the investment remained broadly stable, increasing by 1 per cent from $5.23 billion ( ₹49,718 crore) in Q3 2025.
“The quarterly rebound brought investment close to the peak of $5.66 billion ( ₹53,826 crore) recorded in Q4 2025, followed by a dip to $3.37 billion ( ₹32,042 crore) in Q1 2026,” said IEEFA’s Saloni Sachdeva Michael, Charith Konda and Kaira Rakheja in a recent commentary.
The scale of financing required remains substantial. According to the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE), India’s clean energy transition will require ₹47.5 lakh crore ($500 billion) by 2030. The modest y-o-y growth will have to increase significantly to match the scale of India’s demand, they added.
Top investments in the RE sector during Q3 2026 included entities such as Aditya Birla Renewables, Avaada Group, ReNew, the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank and the Japan Bank for International Cooperation.
India’s growing RE investment profile gets a boost due to low-cost RE generation and a growing manufacturing sector.
For instance, India has achieved utility-scale solar generation costs of $30–35 per megawatt-hour (MWh), or roughly ₹2,840– ₹3,313, which is the lowest in the world.
The average tariffs achieved between 2023 and 2025 stood at around $45 per MWh ( ₹4,260), which was 20 per cent below the average cost of electricity from coal-fired power plants.
India’s renewable energy sector has attracted more than ₹15 lakh crore in investment over the past decade. The country has attracted investments worth $67 billion (about ₹6 lakh crore) over the past two years, including $6.2 billion in foreign direct investment (FDI).
To achieve the 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity target, India needs roughly $220 billion, MNRE Minister Pralhad Joshi said at the recently concluded Bharat RE Summit & Expo 2026.
India has emerged as one of the world’s largest clean-industry markets, ranking second globally by total investment opportunity and third by project count, according to the latest findings from Mission Possible Partnership’s Global Project Tracker, supported by the Industrial Transition Accelerator (ITA).
As clean industry redraws the world’s industrial map, India’s $434 billion total investment opportunity comprises $428 billion in potential investment from announced projects and $6.6 billion secured, placing it at the heart of the shift towards renewables-rich economies.
