climate-energy-9bef911c3c.fulltext:
Waaree’s US Trade Disclosures Put India’s Solar Export Strategy Under Pressure
The solar manufacturer's acknowledgement of shipment-origin reporting errors comes amid separate US customs action, raising concerns over trade compliance, export exposure and India's access to a key clean-energy market
Waaree Energies' disclosure of incorrectly classified solar imports from Vietnam and Malaysia has intensified scrutiny of India's solar trade with the United States, with the issue emerging as a potential risk for exporters navigating increasingly stringent trade regulations. The company acknowledged before the US International Trade Commission (USITC) that certain imports of solar cells and modules from Vietnam and Malaysia had inadvertently been reported as originating in India between 2021 and 2026. The disclosure came as part of a wider US investigation into solar imports from India, Indonesia and Laos.
The development is significant for India's solar manufacturing sector, which is increasingly looking towards overseas markets to absorb expanding domestic production capacity. It also highlights how discrepancies in supply-chain documentation can translate into trade disputes, potential duty liabilities and changes in export strategies.
Origin Reporting Keeps India In Trade Probe
The USITC examined whether imports from the three countries crossed the 3 per cent threshold under US trade law, below which imports are generally considered negligible for such investigations. Waaree and Mundra Solar had argued that removing incorrectly classified shipments from the import data would bring India's share below this threshold, potentially excluding the country from the proceedings. However, after reviewing corrected import figures and customs records, the commission concluded that India's share remained above the prescribed limit.
On 14 October 2026, the USITC determined that imports of crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells, whether or not assembled into modules, from India, Indonesia and Laos had materially injured the US solar manufacturing industry. The development comes alongside a separate enforcement proceeding by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), which upheld an adverse duty-evasion determination on 29 October 2026 concerning a limited set of historical shipments. Waaree disclosed the customs decision to stock exchanges on 2 November 2026 and said it was evaluating legal remedies, including judicial review before the US Court of International Trade.
Export Exposure Drives Order Book Reset
The trade dispute has also begun influencing Waaree's commercial strategy. As of 30 September 2026, the company had removed more than 3 gigawatts (GW) of export contracts from its active reported order book amid growing uncertainty over US trade measures. Following the rationalisation, Waaree's total order book stood at approximately Rs 59,200 crore, representing 25.6 GW of capacity. Domestic orders accounted for 48.4 per cent, while its US manufacturing operations in Texas contributed 43.8 per cent. Direct exports from India made up the remaining 7.8 per cent, down from 24 per cent in the preceding quarter.
For the Indian solar industry, the case highlights the growing importance of supply-chain transparency and regulatory compliance as manufacturers expand their international footprint. Industry observers see localisation, stronger supplier verification and traceable component sourcing as increasingly important to maintaining competitiveness in global markets.
With the US remaining a significant destination for Indian solar manufacturers, the outcome of ongoing trade proceedings could influence investment decisions, export commitments and the economics of overseas expansion.

‘Needs much greater commitment of troops’
NEW DELHI, Nov 14:
India's border with China has become "more alive" and requires a much greater commitment of Indian troops on a sustained basis, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said on Saturday as he listed New Delhi's policy approach to enhance infrastructure along the frontier.

Jaishankar also said that India has bolstered its military capabilities along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) since the deadly clashes in Eastern Ladakh's Galwan Valley in 2020.
His remarks at an interactive session here came amid ongoing efforts by New Delhi and Beijing to normalise their relations that came under severe strain following the over four-year border face-off in Eastern Ladakh.
"Just think about the last few years. How often do you now read - a new tunnel has been built, some new bridges have been built, another airfield has been commissioned. You're getting this news with greater and greater frequency," he said.
"What has happened today is the border with China has become more alive in a way. It has required a much greater commitment of troops on a sustained basis."
"The fact is that the work we had already done allowed that kind of numbers to be deployed out there, and the work we continue to do will maintain those numbers," he said.
After over four years of frosty ties over the eastern Ladakh military standoff, India and China began to repair relations following a meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping in the Russian city of Kazan in October 2024 that took place after the face-off ended.
The talks between Modi and Xi covered a range of issues, including reducing their trade deficit, tackling challenges like terrorism and ensuring fair trade in multilateral platforms.
"I would say when it comes to the border, I would honestly make this point, and I think there's a lot of data and evidence to back it up, which is that the border infrastructure was really neglected till about a decade ago. I mean, people spoke about it, people drew up plan," Jaishankar said.
"If you actually go on the ground and see year-by-year how many kilometres of roads, what was the tunnelling, what was the positioning, I think anybody, and certainly anybody associated with the armed forces dealing with that sector knows the truth," he noted.
Jaishankar added: "It's really been in the last decade that that kind of attention, resources, policy push has been given."
The External Affairs Minister said India's capability to "deploy" its troops on that border has seen "a very marked" improvement.

world-b328d4fdad.headline: US floated idea of Ukraine ceding Donbas for NATO membership, Zelenskiy says
world-b328d4fdad.fulltext:
[Text below is BBC's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The US has not confirmed Zelensky's comments, and a US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties".
The Ukrainian leader's comments came after US envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.
He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.
Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.
Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.
Other Nato members apart from the US are wary of membership for Ukraine - and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees that as unrealistic.
The Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed, too. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.
It is possible the American envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky said recently that the US mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.
Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.
So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public in order to re-open a discussion that had been considered all but closed.
He maintains that the idea is now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security.
It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.
The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.
Hours after Zelensky's remarks, Jared Kushner appeared keen to dampen down any US offer of Nato membership for Ukraine, urging "confidentiality" in a sensitive process.
He said that "maximalist" proposals had been reported from the negotiations, along with "strong political rhetoric".
In what read like a reproach to Kyiv, Kushner referred to "private discussions" aimed at exploring new ideas about ending what he called a "horrible war".
He said the hope was that those ideas might lead to new proposals or breakthroughs.
Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.
It has insisted again that it will not agree to a ceasefire until a final peace deal is in place that would include Ukraine ceding control of those parts of the Donbas Russian troops have not captured, in addition to the Crimean peninsula Moscow annexed illegally in 2014.
The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.
Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service, which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.
Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:20 local time (21:20 GMT) on Saturday, in the first-ever successful catch attempt.

Its generic drugmakers helped make treatments accessible to millions of patients, including those in the US, where low-cost imports have become an important part of the healthcare system.But now that model is under immense pressure, one that could collapse any non-established player in the market and usurp India from its position as the ‘world’s pharmacy’.US president Donald Trump wants to use steep tariffs to push pharmaceutical companies to manufacture generic drugs in the US, a step integral to his America First policy and quest to negate America’s dependence on any external industry. But the blue wave that just swept both chambers of Congress has heavily campaigned on healthcare affordability. Trump’s current proposal will create manufactured inflation and a huge price hike in the cost of medicines, so how do the Democrats keep their campaign promise but also work towards reducing US’s dependence on imported medicines.
The timing currently gives Indian companies a window to assess their options, but it does not remove the uncertainty a lot of manufacturers are almost sure to face. The US is a major export market for Indian generic manufacturers, while generic medicines account for more than 90% of prescriptions filled in the country.The importance of these imports is reflected in the economics of the American drug market. While branded medicines in the US are often more expensive than in comparable countries, unbranded generics are an exception.“For every dollar the other countries on average pay for these drugs, in the US, consumers pay 67 cents. Unbranded generics made up 90 percent of US prescription volume, compared with 41 percent of volume in the other countries,” says Saptarshi Ghosh, a geopolitics analyst.“This is where Indian pharma companies have played an important role in keeping prescription drug prices low,” he says.For some of India’s biggest drugmakers, the US brings in 30 to 50 percent of revenue. Indian pharma exports to the US fell nearly 10 percent to $9.47 billion in FY26, Pharmexcil says, a drop it puts down to price erosion, a high base and inventory corrections. Analysts see Lupin, Aurobindo, Dr Reddy’s, Granules and Glenmark as more exposed, and Sun, Cipla, Zydus and Torrent as better placed. Cipla says 35 to 40 percent of what it sells in the US is made there.A sharp increase in import duties could force companies to absorb additional costs, raise prices, consider moving some production closer to the American market or completely remove themselves from the market if absorption is not an option that works for them.
But lowering insurance premiums through ACA subsidies, restoring Medicaid funding and reducing prescription drug prices are distinct policy interventions. Nor does the existing Medicare drug-price negotiation programme amount to government price-setting for every medicine imported into the US.Under the Inflation Reduction Act, Medicare can negotiate prices for selected high-expenditure drugs that do not face generic or biosimilar competition. Once a generic or biosimilar version is approved and marketed, the original drug can become ineligible for selection or be removed from the programme.The Democrats' proposal to extend negotiated-price savings to people with private insurance would broaden the reach of the existing framework. But it would not automatically bring all Indian-made generic medicines under Medicare price negotiation.For Indian manufacturers, companies with portfolios spanning generics, branded medicines and complex products such as biosimilars may face different kinds of pricing pressure. For manufacturers focused on commodity generics, the more immediate questions concern tariffs, competition, procurement costs and the economics of producing medicines for the American market.But there is a broader shift in American politics and debate that could act as leverage for Indian manufacturers. Democrats and Republicans differ sharply over how to make healthcare affordable, but both have reasons to favour a larger domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing base. For Republicans, reshoring is tied to economic and national security. For Democrats, the argument sits alongside a promise to reduce healthcare costs and strengthen the public health system.The next Congress faces a difficult balance act, especially since the voters have brought them in based on their promises. They need to figure out how to reduce dependence on imported medicines without making those medicines more expensive for American patients.

Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.
The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.
It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Russia has confirmed the meeting. China has yet to react.
No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.
Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.
"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.
She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".
A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation that helped resolve the Cold War.
The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement that included China, which has been building up its arsenal.
Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could create major hurdles and take years.
Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September.
Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.
But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.
Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan.
The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its largest trade partner.
Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.
Earlier this month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media that there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.

deep-tech-3f8a5bc2be.fulltext:
OpenAI reassigns robotics researchers to other teams as general-purpose models might make specialized robotics AI unnecessary
Update –
The opening sentence of this article originally stated that OpenAI was "apparently disbanding its robotics team again." OpenAI has since clarified that it reorganized the team to work more closely with research and product and that robotics work continues. The opening sentence has been updated to reflect this.
OpenAI has reorganized its robotics team, though for different reasons than when it first disbanded the unit in 2020.
Rather than abandoning robotics, the company wants to accelerate it by folding researchers into other teams. Robotics researchers are moving to the main research team under Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams join Greg Brockman's Applied organization.
OpenAI made the decision on such short notice that it had already booked a booth at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin, which then sat empty, Fortune reports. OpenAI apparently believes that general-purpose models like GPT-6 Astra can control robots directly, reducing the need for specialized robotics models.
In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8 percent success rate on simulated robotics tasks, compared to 51 percent for the best specialized models. The tests used a simulated DROID robot, not a physical one.
A new robotics benchmark called StationeryBench compared GPT-6 Astra with Ai2's MolmoAct2 on five tasks involving desk objects on dual-arm YAM robotic arms. Across 200 trials, Astra fully completed 7 out of 100 tasks, while MolmoAct2 didn't complete a single one. Astra's average progress score was 46, compared to 12 for MolmoAct2. In another test, Astra running on a humanoid robot navigated and cleaned up a kitchen.
It remains unclear how much robotics data OpenAI and others incorporated during training. Other large general-purpose models from Anthropic and Google have also made recent progress on robotics tasks. Specialized robotics models may still have advantages in cost and reliability as well as speed and energy consumption, even if they don't generalize as well.
Yoav Artzi, an AI researcher at Cornell University and Google DeepMind, also sees Astra as a major leap in spatial understanding. On the still-unpublished REMAP benchmark, GPT-6 Astra reaches near-human accuracy, according to Artzi. He suspects that OpenAI may have trained the model on large amounts of 3D training data such as Blender scenes.
OpenAI and robots, it's complicated
OpenAI shut down its robotics division in 2020 because, according to co-founder Wojciech Zaremba, the company lacked the training data it needed and large language models were a faster path to AGI. The company rebuilt the team in 2024. CEO Sam Altman is reportedly targeting a first public robot demo for 2027, and OpenAI wants to build its own everyday robots in the long term. But the company also faces heavy financial pressure to focus on its core AI business, where it has lost significant ground to Anthropic.

‘Bulk of issues’ sorted regarding India-US trade deal, says S Jaishankar
The ‘last stretch of concerns remain at the American end’, not New Delhi, the minister said at the ‘Hindustan Times Leadership Summit’.
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on Saturday said that the “bulk of the issues” regarding a trade agreement between India and the United States have been “sorted out” and that the “last stretch of concerns remain at the American end”, not New Delhi.
Jaishankar was speaking at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit.
“In many cases, the concerns are not so much on our side, because the changes have been more on the American side than ours,” said the minister.
After an interim trade deal was agreed upon on February 2, US tariffs on Indian goods would have been reduced to 18% from a combined rate of 50%. The earlier rate of 50% had included a punitive levy of 25% imposed in August 2025 over India’s purchase of Russian oil.
However, negotiations on the final deal were hampered after the US Supreme Court on February 20 struck down global tariffs imposed by Trump, ruling that he had exceeded his authority.
In response, Trump imposed a temporary 10% tariff on goods imported into the US, citing his authority under the 1974 Trade Act. This has left the status of US’ trade deals with countries, including India, unclear.
On Saturday, Jaishankar said that everyone becomes “impatient” during the final stages of any negotiation.
“People want to know what the specific issues are and how long it will take,” he said. “Negotiators do not usually disclose such details during a negotiation.”
During his India visit on October 20, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had said that Washington and India are “very, very close” to signing a trade agreement.
“I would say we are about as close as you can be without having an executed agreement,” he had said.
This had come days after Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on October 5 that the trade talks between India and the US had reached a “plateau” and further concessions might be difficult.

indian-startups-a9c17a4fe5.headline: Jensen Huang’s Exit: How Deep Does NVIDIA’s AI Ecosystem Run In India?
indian-startups-a9c17a4fe5.fulltext: Jensen Huang’s exit from NVIDIA has put the spotlight on the company’s leadership and succession plans. But for India, the more consequential question is what happens to an ecosystem that has increasingly come to depend on the American chipmaker for its AI ambitions. From data centre operators ordering thousands of GPUs to startups building on its software stack, NVIDIA has established relationships across almost every layer of India's AI industry. Its influence extends beyond hardware procurement to cloud infrastructure, developer tools, technical partnerships, startup incubation and even equity investments. It is also helping Indian companies access global investors and customers. The scale of this presence is visible in the country's expanding AI infrastructure ambitions. Some of the key partnerships include Yotta Data Services committing to deploying more than 20,000 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs, while Greenko promoters-backed AM Intelligence (AMI) has announced orders for 29,000 next-generation Rubin GPUs. L&T's Vyoma, meanwhile, is developing a 10,000-GPU AI Factory using NVIDIA's B300 architecture. But these relationships are not identical. Some companies procure hardware, others access NVIDIA's technology through OEMs and systems integrators, while several startups rely primarily on its software and developer ecosystem. India's dependence on NVIDIA runs across three layers: hardware, software and commercial relationships. Competing with NVIDIA and providing alternatives to its Indian partners, therefore, requires more than matching its hardware. Rivals must also replicate its software ecosystem and industry relationships, Sanchit Vir Gogoi, analyst and founder of Greyhound Research, told Inc42. The question is whether Huang's departure changes any of these relationships, and how exposed Indian companies are to a change in NVIDIA's priorities. NVIDIA's Grip On AI Compute India's AI infrastructure buildout is increasingly being shaped around NVIDIA's GPUs. Yotta, Neysa, ESDS, AMI, E2E Networks and L&T Vyoma are among the companies making large commitments to the chipmaker's hardware, although the procurement arrangements and partnerships differ. According to Counterpoint Research, quoted by Moneycontrol, there have been commitments of over $4–5 Bn toward Nvidia's GPU-powered AI data centres. This included both AI stack and infrastructure partnerships. That dependence also has a policy dimension. The IndiaAI Mission's common compute programme relies on a network of empanelled cloud and infrastructure providers. IndiaAI Mission, which had onboarded over 45,000 GPUs by June 2026. By August, it had approved 237 projects for subsidised compute, with 93.18 Lakh GPU hours sanctioned. Any disruption in access to advanced GPUs could therefore affect not just private data centre operators but also the availability and pricing of compute for startups, researchers and government-backed AI projects. The Geopolitical GPU Game Huang's exit has exposed a geopolitical vulnerability in India's AI infrastructure ambitions: its dependence on a company whose access to global markets, political influence and supply chains is now under greater scrutiny. The concern is particularly relevant amid renewed US scrutiny of advanced chip exports. The Biden administration's 2025 AI Diffusion Rule, which had placed India in a middle tier with import caps, was subsequently suspended from enforcement by the Trump administration. However, the formal rescission process remains incomplete, according to a May 2026 Government Accountability Office assessment, as noted by Vipul Agrawal, partner at law firm Clavius Legal. More recently, reports have suggested that the US Commerce Department is considering tighter licensing requirements for advanced chip shipments to seven countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand. India has not been named in the proposed framework so far. Agrawal says India's current position is comparatively favourable, but that does not guarantee uninterrupted access. "On the US Government's published position, India currently enjoys comparatively favourable treatment for buying advanced AI chips, but that is not a guarantee of supply. Suppliers may ask more about where chips are deployed, who the customers are and where the chips may go next, which could slow procurement." He adds that Indian operators must also account for restrictions governing the subsequent transfer or export of controlled hardware. Exports of certain high-performance chips and computers containing these chipsets are only allowed on government authorisation. For Indian neoclouds and data centre operators, the challenge is therefore not limited to securing an initial GPU shipment. They must also understand the ownership structure of their customers, intended use and potential restrictions on overseas customers accessing their infrastructure. “Indian neoclouds and data centre operators must assess their obligations under the US Export Administration Regulations (EAR). This includes verifying the export classification of the GPUs, applicable licensing requirements, and the identity of the supplier, consignee, and end-user,” said Shashi Mathews, partner At CMS INDUSLAW. Indian providers must bear in mind that providing foreign nationals or restricted entities with access to controlled technology or computing power can legally function similarly to exporting the physical item, he added. Who Can Compete With NVIDIA? Meanwhile, alternatives are beginning to emerge. AMD's Instinct accelerators and Google's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) offer competing architectures. The IndiaAI Compute Portal's empanelment table lists 44,077 compute units from 14 bidders: 35,985 NVIDIA units, 5,548 Google Trillium TPUs, 1,096 AMD MI300X and MI325X units, 1,200 AWS Trainium and Inferentia units, and 248 Intel Gaudi units. So does India need to diversify? “Yes, by workload, and with evidence,” said Greyhound Research’s Gogoi. “Inference is where portability is closest to ready, because serving software increasingly hides the accelerator from the application.” Indian startups are also exploring different approaches. Bengaluru-based Turiyam is developing a full-stack compute platform built around inference workloads, CUDA-free middleware and RISC-V hardware. Ziroh Labs, meanwhile, is positioning its Kompact AI runtime as a CPU-first alternative, claiming NVIDIA A100-class inference performance on Intel Xeon processors. These companies are not yet substitutes for NVIDIA's large-scale GPU ecosystem. But they reflect an emerging effort to reduce dependence on a single hardware architecture. The NVIDIA Ecosystem Lock-In Hardware is only one part of NVIDIA's influence. Its software, particularly CUDA, is arguably an even more significant source of competitive advantage. CUDA, NVIDIA's parallel computing platform, allows developers to build applications that run on its GPUs. Over the years, the company has built an extensive ecosystem of libraries, development tools and frameworks around it, including cuDNN, TensorRT and its broader AI Enterprise platform. For companies developing and deploying AI models, this ecosystem reduces the time and effort required to build applications on NVIDIA hardware. Developers can use established frameworks and libraries rather than building infrastructure from scratch. This creates a significant switching cost. A company that has invested years in building its AI applications around CUDA cannot necessarily move to AMD or another accelerator simply by replacing its GPUs. It may have to rewrite parts of its software, optimise workloads and retrain engineering teams. NVIDIA has also expanded its software offerings beyond the underlying computing platform. Its NeMo framework supports the development and customisation of generative AI models, while NIM provides microservices for deploying AI models in production. The company has also developed Nemotron, a family of open models, and tools for data curation and model optimisation. And Indian companies are already using these offerings. NVIDIA has Sarvam AI, Gnani.ai, Chariot, CoRover.ai, and Tech Mahindra among adopters of its NeMo and Nemotron ecosystem. TCS, Infosys and Wipro have also been building enterprise AI solutions using NVIDIA's software stack. This software presence is significant because it creates relationships even with companies that do not directly own or operate large GPU clusters. Will Open Source Survive? Jensen Huang has also championed open source AI models and development tools, an approach that has helped NVIDIA strengthen its position among developers. Notably, NVIDIA announced that it will acquire Huggingface, one of the world’s largest repositories of open source models, for approximately $13 Bn. However, its support for open source is also commercially driven. Open models can be adapted and optimised to run on the hardware most widely available to developers. Given NVIDIA's current market position, this often means its own GPUs and CUDA cores. Rahul Sai Poruri, CEO of FOSS United Foundation, which supports and promotes open source ecosystem in India, believes NVIDIA's strategy to drive open source is unlikely to change dramatically after Huang's departure. "NVIDIA definitely benefits significantly from the existence of open models. If we have more and more closed models, such as Google's Gemini, these models could be optimised specifically for Google's hardware, including its TPUs. Open models, on the other hand, are likely to be optimised for whatever GPU is most widely available to developers. Currently, that is NVIDIA." He added that it could take several years, potentially half a decade or more, for the broader ecosystem to meaningfully reduce its dependence on NVIDIA. Huang's exit may change the company's public positioning or priorities over time. However, its software business, developer relationships and established integrations are institutional assets that are unlikely to disappear with a leadership transition. From Inception To Startup Investments NVIDIA's relationship with India extends beyond selling hardware and software; the company has also been building a pipeline of startups, investors and technology partners that can expand the adoption of its computing platforms. A key part of this strategy is NVIDIA Inception, its global startup programme. The initiative provides early-stage companies with access to technical training, developer tools, preferred pricing on select hardware and software, cloud credits and introductions to potential investors and business partners. The programme is free and does not require startups to give up equity. NVIDIA says it supports more than 4,000 Indian AI startups, making it an important channel for bringing new developers and companies into its ecosystem. More recently, NVIDIA has started making direct equity investments in Indian startups. In August 2026, it participated in a $74 Mn funding tranche for Sarvam AI, becoming the startup's first strategic investor from the global chip industry. The investment came as Sarvam expanded its efforts to build sovereign AI models and applications for Indian languages. NVIDIA also participated in Simplismart's $14 Mn Series B round in October 2026. The startup builds software to help enterprises deploy and optimise AI models and has worked with NVIDIA on technical integrations involving its Dynamo inference software. These investments are important because they go beyond the traditional customer-vendor relationship. NVIDIA is now backing companies that could become significant consumers of its hardware and software, while also helping them develop products and reach customers. indian-startups-2baf5e756b.fulltext:
Before it was thrust into crisis this week, Nvidia was steadily continuing its pace as one of the busiest startup investors around, including backing many of the biggest venture deals of 2026.
The chipmaker and its NVentures arm have participated in more than 120 startup funding deals so far this year, according to Crunchbase data, already topping last year’s record-setting pace and marking its most prolific year yet as a private-company investor.
With co-founder Jensen Huang’s sudden departure this week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs including with employees and a woman U.S. intelligence experts suspect of spying for China, we took a fresh look at where Nvidia and NVentures have been investing and what the future could hold.
A widening investment footprint
Nvidia is the most active corporate investor so far in 2026, an analysis of Crunchbase data shows. It and NVentures together are also among the top 20 most active investors in startups this year overall.
Nvidia’s startup investments this year total 121 and span AI model developers, data center operators, robotics startups and healthcare companies. That continues the broad approach we examined last year, when the company and its venture arm participated in 91 known startup financings, up from 54 the year prior.
The largest Nvidia-backed deals in 2026 include OpenAI’s Series G, which closed at $122 billion in March, and Anthropic’s $30 billion Series G in February. (Those figures represent the entire rounds, including other investors’ contributions, rather than Nvidia’s individual checks.)
The company also participated in a $3.9 billion September Series F for AI infrastructure provider Crusoe and a roughly $3.5 billion September Series D for model developer Mistral AI.
Of course, large as those deals are, Nvidia’s startup bets represent a small fraction of the company’s incredible market capitalization. Even as its share price tumbled this week with Huang’s departure and the surrounding news, Nvidia’s valuation remains close to $4 trillion.
Beyond the biggest AI labs
NVentures’ activity shows how far that investment footprint extends beyond the best-known model developers.
The venture arm’s larger bets this year include robot intelligence developer Skild AI’s $1.4 billion January Series C, and autonomous driving startup Waabi’s $750 million Series C in the same month. It also backed two rounds for Bedrock Robotics, which develops technology to automate construction equipment: a $270 million Series B in February and a $600 million Series C in October. Its healthcare investments included a $150 million April Series E for medical imaging AI company Aidoc.
As in years past, Nvidia and NVentures usually participate alongside other investors. The company or its venture arm are listed as lead or co-lead investors in about 1 in 5 of its deals this year, per Crunchbase data.
For startups, Nvidia’s value as an investor also extends beyond its deep pockets. NVentures describes its offering as access to technical teams, technology integrations and help reaching customers.
The question of what comes next
Nvidia’s new leadership could bring a different approach to risk. Before this week’s news, CFO and now interim CEO Collette Kress had pushed back on Huang’s increasingly large AI investments, Reuters reported this week, citing two people familiar with the matter.
Nvidia’s board has said it expects operations, customer commitments and its product roadmap to continue without interruption. That assurance leaves the pace of future investments an open question. With earnings scheduled for Nov. 17, founders and investors will be watching for signs of how much of Huang’s investment playbook continues under new leadership.

Modi's office summons telecom secretary over use of fake court orders, officials say
NEW DELHI, Nov 14 : Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's office summoned the telecommunications secretary on Saturday to explain how officials ordered the takedown of more than 100 websites based on fake court orders, two government officials said.
The intervention from Modi's office signals intensifying scrutiny after Reuters reported on Wednesday that telecom officials directed internet providers to block 129 illegal betting websites based on fake High Court orders which were emailed to officials by people posing as lawyers.
While online betting is illegal in India, the case has raised concerns that a lack of safeguards in India's content-takedown system could allow falsified court documents to be used to block legitimate websites.
The findings have triggered a criminal investigation by state police into potential forgery and cheating by unidentified people.
Modi's office summoned Telecom Secretary Amit Agrawal to appear and explain the lapse, cutting short Agrawal's trip to another state, said the two government officials with knowledge of the matter.
Agrawal is the most senior bureaucrat in the telecommunications ministry, which oversees everyone from big telecom operators to internet providers.
"The action taken by the Department of Telecommunications against betting accounts was carried out through the relevant field officers," one of the officials said.
Agrawal, his ministry and Modi's office did not respond to requests for comment.
Court precedents generated using AI have caused concerns among judges the world over. India's Supreme Court in July set aside a tribunal's orders that relied on non-existent judgments, and a US judge recently disqualified lawyers over use of fabricated legal citations.
On Friday, Reuters reported that the telecoms ministry had initiated an internal investigation into the alleged fraud, while police have sought ministry records as part of a criminal investigation.
The two state court orders flagged as fake by Reuters, based on comments from police and the court registry, contained fabricated court logos and seals, as well as a fake QR code.
They were available publicly on the Department of Telecommunications' website for months, along with correspondence that showed government officials ordering internet providers to remove the websites.
On Saturday, one of the fake court orders was still accessible on the government's website, while one had been removed.
Amid growing concerns over fake orders, India's Supreme Court justices last year said such fabrication "bearing forged signatures of Judges strikes at the very foundation of public trust" and "such grave criminal acts cannot be treated as ordinary or routine offences".

world-1476d670af.headline: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
world-1476d670af.fulltext:
US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
- Published
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The US has not confirmed Zelensky's comments, and a US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties".
The Ukrainian leader's comments came after US envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.
He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.
Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.
Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.
Other Nato members apart from the US are wary of membership for Ukraine - and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees that as unrealistic.
The Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed, too. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.
It is possible the American envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky said recently that the US mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.
Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.
So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public in order to re-open a discussion that had been considered all but closed.
He maintains that the idea is now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security.
It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.
The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.
Hours after Zelensky's remarks, Jared Kushner appeared keen to dampen down any US offer of Nato membership for Ukraine, urging "confidentiality" in a sensitive process.
He said that "maximalist" proposals had been reported from the negotiations, along with "strong political rhetoric".
In what read like a reproach to Kyiv, Kushner referred to "private discussions" aimed at exploring new ideas about ending what he called a "horrible war".
He said the hope was that those ideas might lead to new proposals or breakthroughs.
Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.
It has insisted again that it will not agree to a ceasefire until a final peace deal is in place that would include Ukraine ceding control of those parts of the Donbas Russian troops have not captured, in addition to the Crimean peninsula Moscow annexed illegally in 2014.
The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.
Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service, which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.
Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

beyond-your-beat-dc1f5a5894.headline: Italy fines Meta $880m over photo privacy
beyond-your-beat-dc1f5a5894.fulltext:
Italy fines Meta $880m over photo privacy
Regulator said Meta’s ‘lack of cooperation’ and the large number of people affected contributed to size of the fine.
Italian regulators have fined Meta 805 million euros ($887m) for accessing users’ photos without their consent.
The Facebook app on Android devices “accessed photos, videos and associated metadata stored on Italian users’ smartphones without specific consent and without informing them”, Garante, the Italian data privacy authority, said Saturday.
The issue relates specifically to the “Get suggestions from gallery when browsing Facebook” feature, which suggests photos and videos from the phone’s gallery for posting while browsing.
This feature violates the Italian law implementing the EU’s ePrivacy directive, the authority said.
Garante said the app’s process for collecting consent is too generic and does not allow users to fully understand the specific permissions they are allowing by accepting. The suggestions option was also enabled by default.
The figure of 805 million euros is by far the largest fine ever imposed by the Italian regulator.
Garante said Meta must fix the unclear consent notification and disable it being set by default, suggesting that roughly 20 million Italian Android users could have been affected by it.
The regulator also highlighted a “lack of cooperation” by Meta and said an earlier violation, which resulted in a 2019 fine, was a contributing factor in their decision.
The amount is roughly 0.47 percent of Meta’s global turnover.
The proceedings did not address the possible use of content to train artificial intelligence, which Meta denies.
Meta has not yet publicly commented on the matter, and it has the right to appeal the regulator’s decision.

global-economics-69644fc7b5.headline: A bitter pill: Indian pharma industry, Trump’s tariff and a Congress that campaigned on cheaper care

- A bitter pill: Indian pharma industry, Trump’s tariff and a Congress that campaigned on cheaper care
Trending
India isn’t a country known for its quality of life, but it is a country that makes the ability to fight for that life surprisingly affordable. A life-saving blood cancer drug that costs around Rs 300 per pill in India can cost as much as Rs 85,000 for the same medication in the US.For decades, India’s pharmaceutical industry has built its global position on a simple formula of affordability. Its generic drugmakers helped make treatments accessible to millions of patients, including those in the US, where low-cost imports have become an important part of the healthcare system.But now that model is under immense pressure, one that could collapse any non-established player in the market and usurp India from its position as the ‘world’s pharmacy’.US president Donald Trump wants to use steep tariffs to push pharmaceutical companies to manufacture generic drugs in the US, a step integral to his America First policy and quest to negate America’s dependence on any external industry. But the blue wave that just swept both chambers of Congress has heavily campaigned on healthcare affordability. Trump’s current proposal will create manufactured inflation and a huge price hike in the cost of medicines, so how do the Democrats keep their campaign promise but also work towards reducing US’s dependence on imported medicines.
The timing currently gives Indian companies a window to assess their options, but it does not remove the uncertainty a lot of manufacturers are almost sure to face. The US is a major export market for Indian generic manufacturers, while generic medicines account for more than 90% of prescriptions filled in the country.The importance of these imports is reflected in the economics of the American drug market. While branded medicines in the US are often more expensive than in comparable countries, unbranded generics are an exception.“For every dollar the other countries on average pay for these drugs, in the US, consumers pay 67 cents. Unbranded generics made up 90 percent of US prescription volume, compared with 41 percent of volume in the other countries,” says Saptarshi Ghosh, a geopolitics analyst.“This is where Indian pharma companies have played an important role in keeping prescription drug prices low,” he says.For some of India’s biggest drugmakers, the US brings in 30 to 50 percent of revenue. Indian pharma exports to the US fell nearly 10 percent to $9.47 billion in FY26, Pharmexcil says, a drop it puts down to price erosion, a high base and inventory corrections. Analysts see Lupin, Aurobindo, Dr Reddy’s, Granules and Glenmark as more exposed, and Sun, Cipla, Zydus and Torrent as better placed. Cipla says 35 to 40 percent of what it sells in the US is made there.A sharp increase in import duties could force companies to absorb additional costs, raise prices, consider moving some production closer to the American market or completely remove themselves from the market if absorption is not an option that works for them.
But lowering insurance premiums through ACA subsidies, restoring Medicaid funding and reducing prescription drug prices are distinct policy interventions. Nor does the existing Medicare drug-price negotiation programme amount to government price-setting for every medicine imported into the US.Under the Inflation Reduction Act, Medicare can negotiate prices for selected high-expenditure drugs that do not face generic or biosimilar competition. Once a generic or biosimilar version is approved and marketed, the original drug can become ineligible for selection or be removed from the programme.The Democrats' proposal to extend negotiated-price savings to people with private insurance would broaden the reach of the existing framework. But it would not automatically bring all Indian-made generic medicines under Medicare price negotiation.For Indian manufacturers, companies with portfolios spanning generics, branded medicines and complex products such as biosimilars may face different kinds of pricing pressure. For manufacturers focused on commodity generics, the more immediate questions concern tariffs, competition, procurement costs and the economics of producing medicines for the American market.But there is a broader shift in American politics and debate that could act as leverage for Indian manufacturers. Democrats and Republicans differ sharply over how to make healthcare affordable, but both have reasons to favour a larger domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing base. For Republicans, reshoring is tied to economic and national security. For Democrats, the argument sits alongside a promise to reduce healthcare costs and strengthen the public health system.The next Congress faces a difficult balance act, especially since the voters have brought them in based on their promises. They need to figure out how to reduce dependence on imported medicines without making those medicines more expensive for American patients.

global-economics-9f850f7eab.headline: Jensen Huang spy scandal puts Howard Lutnick in focus after Scott Bessent's remarks: What are his family’s Nvidia ties?
global-economics-9f850f7eab.fulltext:
Sayantani BiswasPublished14 Nov 2026, 07:38 PM IST US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has put Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick under fresh scrutiny over the Trump administration's handling of suspected Nvidia chip smuggling to China. Lutnick's family business ties to Nvidia and its AI partners have added another layer to the controversy. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's remarks about the handling of suspected Nvidia chip smuggling to China have brought Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick into the spotlight. Bessent said several government departments had supported placing Singapore-based Megaspeed on a restricted entity list for months, pointing to the Commerce Department as the agency responsible for taking action. The comments have renewed attention on Lutnick's former Wall Street firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, which is now run by his sons, Brandon and Kyle Lutnick. The firm has reported investments in Nvidia and helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for companies connected to the chipmaker's artificial intelligence business. There is no evidence that the family's business interests influenced Lutnick's government decisions or that his sons received confidential intelligence. Before joining Donald Trump's administration in February 2025, Lutnick headed Cantor Fitzgerald. He later transferred his ownership stake to his children through trusts. A CNBC analysis of securities filings found that Cantor's reported Nvidia shareholding fell by nearly 50% between September 2025 and March 2026. At the end of 2024, the firm disclosed more than 3.5 million Nvidia shares worth approximately $479 million. Their value climbed to $652 million by September 2025. However, the reported share count fell to three million in December and 1.78 million by March 2026. Cantor has not publicly explained the reduction. It has said the Nvidia positions reported in regulatory filings largely reflected client swap transactions rather than substantial standalone investments. The controversy goes beyond Cantor's investments. According to Axios, Lutnick received a highly classified intelligence warning about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's alleged links to a suspected Chinese spy. The Commerce Secretary also faced pressure from White House and intelligence officials to take action against Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company suspected of helping channel Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China. Axios reported that Lutnick repeatedly resisted efforts to crack down on the company, despite Trump authorising fresh export restrictions. Bessent's comments have exposed divisions within the administration over the issue. He said the Treasury, Defence and State departments, along with the US Trade Representative's office, had supported placing Megaspeed on the restricted entity list for months. Cantor's business connections extend beyond its reported Nvidia shareholding. In September, the firm hosted Huang and other senior Nvidia executives at investor meetings in New York. Its analysts subsequently maintained an overweight rating on Nvidia shares, describing the chipmaker as an attractive investment. The firm has also helped finance companies in Nvidia's AI ecosystem. In May 2026, Nvidia announced a five-year cloud computing agreement worth $3.4 billion with Australian company IREN. Days later, IREN announced a $3 billion convertible bond offering, with Cantor among seven banks arranging the deal. Cantor also advised AI infrastructure developer Lancium on a $600 million financing deal for its data centre campus in Abilene, Texas. The project is connected to Stargate, the AI infrastructure initiative backed by OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle. The overlap between Lutnick's government responsibilities and his family's financial connections has attracted attention from ethics experts and lawmakers. Richard Painter, a former White House chief ethics lawyer under George W Bush, told CNBC there was no proof Lutnick had shared confidential information with Cantor Fitzgerald. However, he said the appearance of a potential conflict was concerning. Democratic lawmakers have also called for greater scrutiny of whether the Lutnick family could benefit from the administration's AI infrastructure policies. The White House continues to back Lutnick. An official told Reuters that Trump retains complete confidence in the Commerce Secretary. So far, there is no evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance knowledge of intelligence warnings about Huang or that Cantor's business interests influenced government decisions.
